semantic_text: or centuries, scientists have used small animal models to study everything from how genes work to how diseases develop. And these pint-sized creatures continue to play important roles in scientific discoveries of all kinds, including vision research.

plain_text:
Small animals teach researchers big lessons
about how vision works, how it can go wrong
(and why), and new ways to treat eye diseases.
semantic_text: Small animals teach researchers big lessons about how vision works, how it can go wrong (and why), and new ways to treat eye diseases.

plain_text:
In the early 1900s, a young graduate student named
Mildred Hoge discovered a group of fruit flies with
eyes that were unusually small...or missing completely.
She mapped the gene responsible for this mutation and
named it eyeless . Her later research with fruit flies showed
that this gene plays a key role in how their eyes and optic
nerves develop.
semantic_text: In the early 1900s, a young graduate student named Mildred Hoge discovered a group of fruit flies with eyes that were unusually small...or missing completely. She mapped the gene responsible for this mutation and named it eyeless . Her later research with fruit flies showed that this gene plays a key role in how their eyes and optic nerves develop.

plain_text:
Almost a century later, scientists discovered that humans
have their own version of the eyeless gene, called PAX6.
Genetic mutations that affect PAX6 can lead to significant
issues such as cataracts and aniridia (a condition that
affects the iris of the eye).
semantic_text: Almost a century later, scientists discovered that humans have their own version of the eyeless gene, called PAX6. Genetic mutations that affect PAX6 can lead to significant issues such as cataracts and aniridia (a condition that affects the iris of the eye).

plain_text:
NIH-supported researchers continue to study fruit fly
development, asking questions like, “What makes an eye
an eye?” and “What keeps it from turning into some other
body part?
semantic_text: NIH-supported researchers continue to study fruit fly development, asking questions like, “What makes an eye an eye?” and “What keeps it from turning into some other body part?

plain_text:
Fruit flies share about 60%
of their genes with humans.
semantic_text: Fruit flies share about 60% of their genes with humans.

plain_text:
Justin Kumar, Ph.D., studies and teaches developmental
biology at Indiana University, Bloomington. He uses fruit
fly models to study how a cell becomes one kind of tissue
(like an eye) and not another (like a wing or an antenna).
PAX6 provides instructions for making proteins that
drive tissue development in the fruit fly eye by turning
on “eye” genes and turning off “non-eye” genes. But just
changing PAX6 on its own doesn’t let a cell become
any type of tissue.
semantic_text: Justin Kumar, Ph.D., studies and teaches developmental biology at Indiana University, Bloomington. He uses fruit fly models to study how a cell becomes one kind of tissue (like an eye) and not another (like a wing or an antenna). PAX6 provides instructions for making proteins that drive tissue development in the fruit fly eye by turning on “eye” genes and turning off “non-eye” genes. But just changing PAX6 on its own doesn’t let a cell become any type of tissue.

plain_text:
Dr. Kumar discovered that PAX6 proteins work together
with another type of protein (called an epigenetic
enzyme) to control how DNA is used in cells. This helps
cells decide what kind of tissue they will become. He and
his team found a way to study this process by turning
off or “knocking out” both proteins at the same time.
Suddenly, eye tissue could turn into all sorts of things—
including a wing!
semantic_text: Dr. Kumar discovered that PAX6 proteins work together with another type of protein (called an epigenetic enzyme) to control how DNA is used in cells. This helps cells decide what kind of tissue they will become. He and his team found a way to study this process by turning off or “knocking out” both proteins at the same time. Suddenly, eye tissue could turn into all sorts of things— including a wing!

plain_text:
By looking at the changes to the modified cell,
Dr. Kumar can tease out what makes a tissue one type
versus another.
semantic_text: By looking at the changes to the modified cell, Dr. Kumar can tease out what makes a tissue one type versus another.
